newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to lobby China for defector's safe passage.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to lobby China for defector's safe passage.

text.p: South Korea's foreign minister plans to lobby China to secure the safe passage from Beijing of a top North Korean official seeking asylum, Seoul officials said on Thursday.

Yoo Chong-ha will leave for Singapore later on Thursday for talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen at a gathering of Southeast Asian and European officials in a bid to resolve a diplomatic crisis over Hwang Jang-yop.
Yoo's special advisor, Kim Ha-jung, flew to Beijing for separate talks with Chinese officials.

South Korean officials said Hwang, 73, a senior aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, remained a political refugee at the consular section of the Beijing embassy one day after arriving by taxi with his assistant Kim Dok-hong.
Dozens of Chinese soldiers cordoned off the building in Beijing's embassy district.
Seoul officials said the North would almost certainly pressure Beijing, one of Stalinist North Korea's few allies, not to allow Hwang to head for South Korea.
They said North Korea's suggestion that South Korean authorities kidnapped Hwang indicated Pyongyang would put up a fight to get him back.
Seoul rejected as "preposterous" any idea it coerced Hwang to defect.
Hwang, ranked 24th in Pyongyang's power structure by Seoul officials, is one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party.
"Such an absurd reaction by the North does not come as a surprise as that has been their usual tactic," National Unification ministry spokesman Kang Ho-yang said.
Beijing is caught in a wrangle between socialist ally North Korea and the capitalist South, which has become an important trading partner and source of investment.

In Beijing, South Korean embassy officials accused North Koreans of trying to force their way into the consular office on Wednesday night. They said Chinese police on guard prevented the North Koreans from entering.
An embassy spokesman said he believed that North Korean officials were still lurking around the office compound.
A Seoul defence ministry official said South Korea's military had heightened vigilance in view of North Korea's "unpredictability".
"The military leadership is carefully analysing the situation and working out possible scenarios to prepare for any contingencies," he said.
South Korea said Hwang was the highest ranking Pyongyang official ever to seek asylum in South Korea, and analysts said his defection indicated cracks in the Stalinist hierarchy.

Hwang, in charge of the North Korean communist party's foreign policy, played a leading role in shaping the policy of juche, a brand of fanatic self-reliance providing the ideological underpinning for the world's last Stalinist state.
A Pyongyang foreign ministry statement threatened unspecified countermeasures against South Korea, and called on China to take "appropriate measures".
The defection row broke four days before the much-heralded 55th birthday of Kim, son of the late president Kim Il-sung, who built a personality cult around the juche creed.
South Korea's Chosun Ilbo newspaper printed a letter attacking Kim Jong-il that it said was written by Hwang. South Korean officials said they were treating it with caution.
"The 'ever-so-great general' has come to believe that he is really a genius after all the idolatry showered on him praising him as a great genius," said the letter.
"How can a society where people, workers, farmers, and intellectuals starve to death be a socialist society?"
Despite the crisis, South Korea said it would respond to a World Food Programme appeal for $41.6 million in new food aid for North Korea.
The United States said it would join the appeal by the U.N. agency to raise 100,000 metric tonnes of food aid.
